title: The national polls are right—Reform is in trouble
gist: Kellner reads Labour's comfortable Greater Manchester mayoral win — Bev Craig beating Reform's Sian Astley, with Labour up 23 points on its May council vote and Reform down 10 — plus 87 council byelections since May in which Reform won only 19 seats on a 23 per cent vote share, as confirmation that Reform's national decline is real rather than a local Burnham effect.

insights.claim: Labour's Bev Craig beat Reform's Sian Astley comfortably on first preferences in the Greater Manchester mayoral race, defeating the expectation that a Reform mayor would be the price of returning Andy Burnham to parliament.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: The feared Labour downside from the Burnham succession did not materialise — removes a tail risk from UK political forecasts.
insights.locator: So much for the fears that a Reform UK mayor

insights.claim: Against the correct comparator — May's Greater Manchester council elections, where Reform took 31 per cent and 104 of 214 seats to Labour's 24 per cent and 35 seats — Labour was 23 points up and Reform 10 points down on first preferences.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: A 33-point swing in three months in the same electorate; the single hardest number establishing the direction of travel.
insights.locator: The more relevant comparison is with the votes

insights.claim: The combined progressive vote rose from 52 per cent in May to 62 per cent, while the right-of-centre vote including Restore fell from 41 to 37 per cent — a bloc-level shift, not just a Labour-Reform switch.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Distinguishes genuine realignment from vote-splitting: the entire right-of-centre bloc shrank.

insights.claim: Craig's first-preference share fell well short of Burnham's two years ago because he had a substantial personal vote and Labour was riding high nationally — so the win understates rather than overstates the underlying swing's cleanliness.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Guards against over-reading the headline: the correct baseline is May 2026, not the Burnham-era peak.
insights.locator: True, her first-preference vote share fell well short

insights.claim: The supplementary vote system structurally works better for mainstream candidates and worse for extreme ones — a reusable rule for forecasting any preferential-ballot contest.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Portable model: wherever preferential systems apply, insurgent parties underperform their first-preference share.
insights.quote: it works better for mainstream candidates, and worse for extreme ones

insights.claim: Almost 170,000 voters backed one of the bottom five candidates and 103,000 of them cast a second vote for Labour or Reform; Labour took 73 per cent of Green and Lib Dem first preferences while Reform took only 52 per cent of Restore and Conservative ones.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Transfer efficiency is the mechanism: Labour converts allied votes at 73 per cent versus Reform's 52 per cent, a durable structural disadvantage for Reform.
insights.locator: Almost 170,000 voters backed one of the bottom five

insights.claim: Craig gained 13,000 more votes than Astley in the second-preference round, so the system amplified rather than merely preserved Labour's lead.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Quantifies the mechanical penalty the ballot design imposes on the insurgent party.
insights.locator: The supplementary vote also helped Labour

insights.claim: Some Conservative second preferences went to Craig rather than Astley, which the author treats as further evidence that preferential voting hurts the extremes even within the right-of-centre bloc.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Tory-to-Labour transfers indicate Reform is not automatically inheriting Conservative decline.
insights.quote: that underlines further the fact that preferential voting hurts the extremes

themes.theme: Reform's national decline in hard data

insights.claim: Reform's local election performance has decayed on a clear track: 41 per cent of seats and a 32 per cent national equivalent vote share in May 2025, down to 29 per cent of seats and 27 per cent vote share this year, and 23 per cent across 87 byelections since.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: A three-point sequential decline across three independent measurement windows — the core evidentiary spine of the bear case on Reform.
insights.locator: In the local elections in May 2025

insights.claim: Across 87 local council byelections since May, Reform won just 19 — a 22 per cent success rate on a 23 per cent vote share — leaving it level with the Conservatives and Lib Dems rather than dominant.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Reform has lost first-mover status on the right; its seat yield now matches the parties it was supposed to replace.
insights.locator: Since this year’s May elections there have been 87 local council byelections

insights.claim: Reform's seat count is highly sensitive to small vote-share moves: at 32 per cent it dominated county after county, but at 27 per cent its victories became patchy — a non-linear seat-conversion curve.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Under first-past-the-post a five-point slippage collapses Reform's seat yield disproportionately — the key sensitivity for general election modelling.
insights.locator: It’s worth noting the way that Reform’s seat numbers are sensitive

insights.claim: Reform's byelection vote trajectory tracks its national poll rating almost precisely, validating the polls against actual cast votes rather than stated intention.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Removes the standard 'polls understate Reform' objection — real ballots and polls now agree.
insights.quote: The trajectory of Reform’s votes tracks the trajectory of Reform’s poll rating almost precisely.

insights.claim: Labour gained two wards from Reform in Thurrock on 24th July — an area Farage was counting on to break through at the next general election — suggesting Burnham's arrival in Downing Street has dragged Reform down further.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Reform is losing ground in its own designated target seats, the most damaging kind of decline for a breakthrough narrative.
insights.quote: an area that Farage was counting on to help his party break through at the next general election
insights.locator: Indeed, Burnham has reason to hope

insights.claim: Turnout in the Manchester mayoral contest was just 25 per cent, so the author explicitly cautions against over-interpreting the single result and leans on the 87-byelection sample instead.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: The honest caveat: the mayoral headline is thin evidence, the byelection aggregate is the real signal.

insights.claim: The three Manchester-area contests — Gorton & Denton, Makerfield and the mayoralty — are argued not to be exceptional 'Burnhamland' results, so the national polls showing Reform in trouble should be believed.
insights.speaker: Peter Kellner
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the consensus that Reform's polling weakness is a local artefact — the article's central contrarian call.
insights.quote: The national polls are right. Reform is in trouble.
insights.locator: All in all, Reform’s recent trio of disappointments
